analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare pharmacy benefit managers to disclose drug prices, rebates, and their own profits to insurers and auditors.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan PBM transparency bill backed by the Senate Finance chair and ranking member never received a committee vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) are the middlemen that negotiate drug prices and manage drug benefits for Medicare drug plans. This bill would force PBMs to report detailed, itemized data to insurers and Medicare each year: what every drug cost, what rebates were paid, how much revenue the PBM and its affiliated pharmacies kept, when the PBM steered prescriptions to its own pharmacies, and when a plan covered a pricier brand drug over a cheaper generic. It would also give insurers the right to audit their PBMs, and make PBMs pay any fines caused by their own reporting failures. The bill never got a vote; it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers. The reporting would expose spread pricing, rebate retention, steering to PBM-owned pharmacies, and formulary choices that favor expensive brand drugs over cheaper generics, giving plan sponsors and Medicare the information to push costs down. Independent community pharmacies would also benefit from disclosure of PBM affiliate steering.

how_it_helps.text: PBMs must file an annual itemized report covering every drug dispensed: claims, out-of-pocket spending, rebates, pharmacy reimbursement rates, and total manufacturer-derived revenue retained by the PBM and its affiliates.

Where a PBM owns retail, mail-order, or specialty pharmacies, it must disclose what share of prescriptions went to its own pharmacies and compare the costs paid at affiliate versus non-affiliate pharmacies.
Plans must report when a cheaper generic or biosimilar was excluded, put on a higher-cost tier, or restricted while the pricier brand-name drug got better coverage, with a written justification.
Plan sponsors may audit their PBM at least annually, the PBM cannot restrict the auditor's selection, and the PBM must reimburse the plan for any civil penalty caused by the PBM's reporting failures.

analysis.who_pays: PBMs and their corporate parents, who bear the cost of extensive annual reporting and face exposure of practices like spread pricing, rebate retention, and steering to affiliated pharmacies. Drug plans take on new certification duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and their corporate parents

drawbacks.text: The disclosures are not public. The bill restricts the Secretary and oversight bodies from releasing information that identifies a specific PBM, plan, or drug price, so beneficiaries never directly see the data; the benefit depends entirely on plans and Medicare acting on it.
The bill creates reporting and compliance costs for PBMs and drug plans with no guarantee prices fall; it compels transparency but does not itself cap prices or ban any PBM practice.
It also directs the GAO to study whether federal and state PBM reporting requirements overlap, an acknowledgment that more layered reporting may add administrative burden across the system.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a modest transparency measure, not a price-control bill. Its real value is arming plan sponsors and Medicare with data on PBM profits, affiliate steering, and brand-over-generic formulary choices, which could pressure costs down over time. Its main weakness is that the data stays confidential, so the public cannot verify anything itself, and compliance costs are real even if small relative to PBM revenues. On balance the benefits plausibly outweigh the costs, but the bill alone would not directly lower anyone's drug bill.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a markup or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto introduced the Medicare PBM Accountability Act on July 12, 2023, with original cosponsors Sens. Tillis, Wyden, and Crapo.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day; the action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action afterward.
The referral went to a committee whose chair (Wyden) and ranking member (Crapo) were both original cosponsors, yet the bill still never advanced.
The bill would have applied to plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, had it become law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest PBMs and their corporate parents, which avoided new disclosure, audit, and penalty obligations, and drug plans that would have taken on certification duties.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large PBMs and their parent companies

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx and their parent companies)
industries.note: The bill would force PBMs to itemize what they retain in rebates and fees, disclose steering to their own pharmacies, and submit to audits and penalties. PBMs profit from opaque pricing and rebate retention, so transparency directly threatens that revenue, and the bill died without a vote.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D insurers and plan sponsors
industries.note: Sponsors gain audit rights and detailed PBM data, but must certify compliance and take on new oversight duties. Many large sponsors own PBMs, so the disclosure cuts against their own affiliates.

Plans must disclose when a cheaper generic or biosimilar was excluded or given worse coverage than a pricier brand drug, with written justification, which could shift volume toward lower-cost products.

Disclosure of the share of prescriptions steered to PBM-affiliated pharmacies and of reimbursement differences between affiliate and non-affiliate pharmacies could ease the reimbursement squeeze on independent drugstores.
